hops.title: The rattlesnake tail that never fuses into tetanus
hops.text: A western diamondback rattlesnake can shake its tail for hours at close to ninety cycles a second. Drive one of your calf's motor units that fast and its twitches would blend into steady force. A rattle needs a separate pulse of force on every shake. The snake's shaker muscles, like the toadfish swimbladder muscles behind its two-hundred-hertz boatwhistle call, keep every twitch separate: calcium is released and cleared very fast, and the force-making proteins let go quickly. About a quarter of each shaker fibre's volume is calcium-storing membrane, and another quarter is mitochondria. Electrical recordings suggest each of the snake's six shaker muscles may be a single motor unit.

sources.citation: Schaeffer, Conley & Lindstedt, J. Exp. Biol. 199(Pt 2):351-358 (1996)
Rome et al., Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 93(15):8095-8100 (1996)

image.caption: Rattlesnake shaker muscles deliver a separate force pulse nearly ninety times a second, for hours.

hops.title: The Pinocchio illusion: vibrating a tendon to grow a nose
hops.text: In 1972, physiologists vibrated volunteers' biceps or triceps tendons at one hundred hertz. While the muscle was contracting, people misjudged their elbow angle by up to forty degrees, feeling the joint as if the vibrated muscle had been stretched. The vibration drives the spindle endings directly, mimicking stretch. In 1988, James Lackner showed it can also distort perceived body shape. Close your eyes, hold the tip of your nose, and have the biceps tendon vibrated: the spindles report an arm straightening and a hand moving away, while the fingertip still feels the nose. In some people, the brain reconciles the two by deciding the nose is growing.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student with closed eyes sits in a chair holding the tip of their nose while a small handheld vibration device rests against the inside of their bent elbow.
image.caption: Vibrating the biceps tendon fakes a spindle stretch signal, so a held nose can feel as if it grows.

hops.title: Newborn stepping that was never switched off
hops.text: A newborn held upright with the feet on a table marches in an alternating rhythm. By about two months this stepping usually fades, and it was widely believed that the maturing cortex had switched off a primitive reflex. Esther Thelen and her colleagues tested a plainer explanation: heavy legs. Lying on their backs, babies keep making the same kicking movement for months. In four-week-old infants, small weights strapped to the legs cut stepping by about a third, and lowering the legs into a tank of warm water nearly doubled it. As the authors pointed out, water should not release cortical inhibition.

sources.citation: Thelen, Fisher & Ridley-Johnson, Infant Behav. Dev. 7(4):479-493 (1984)
Thelen, Fisher, Ridley-Johnson & Griffin, Dev. Psychobiol. 15(5):447-453 (1982)
Adolph & Franchak, Wiley Interdiscip. Rev. Cogn. Sci. 8(1-2):e1430 (2017)

image.caption: Buoyed by warm water, four-week-old infants nearly doubled their stepping; small leg weights cut it by a third.

audio.title: Rattlesnakes, a high ledge and a two-belt treadmill
audio.transcript:
Here are three true stories about the spinal machinery in this lesson: a rattlesnake, a high ledge in Vancouver, and babies on a treadmill with two belts.

First, the rattlesnake. In this lesson, twitches that come close together ride on top of one another until they blend into a smooth, fused tetanus. Steady force is what you want when you carry a bag of groceries, and in everyday contractions your motor units firing out of step smooth it further. A western diamondback rattlesnake wants the opposite: a separate pulse of force on every shake. A diamondback can shake its rattle continuously for hours at close to ninety cycles a second. If its tail-shaker muscles produced steady force, they would lose the pulses that swing the rattle back and forth. In nineteen ninety-six, two research groups looked at how these very fast muscles avoid that. The rattlesnake's shaker muscles, and the swimbladder muscles a toadfish uses for its boatwhistle call at around two hundred cycles a second, release and clear calcium very fast, and their force-making proteins let go quickly, so each spike stays its own twitch. Electrical recordings even suggest that each of the snake's six shaker muscles may be a single motor unit.

Second, a hydraulic lift at the University of British Columbia. You know that muscle spindles report stretch, and that gamma motor neurons can set how sensitive they are. Researchers there wanted to know whether people turn that sensitivity up when a fall would really hurt. They had volunteers stand at the edge of a raised platform, three point two meters up in a twenty thirteen study and three point five meters up in a twenty eighteen study. In the twenty eighteen study, a tap on the Achilles tendon produced a reflex about seventeen percent bigger at the high edge than when standing low and away from it. In a separate test, the calf was stretched at different speeds. In the twenty-two of forty volunteers whose quick stretch reflex tracked stretch speed, the reflex rose more steeply with speed at the edge, by about thirty-six percent on average. And in the twenty thirteen study, an electrically evoked reflex, the H reflex, which skips the spindle and stimulates the sensory axons directly, did not change. That pattern points at the spindle. Nobody recorded gamma motor neurons in these experiments, so the evidence is indirect, but the results suggest the nervous system turns up spindle sensitivity when a fall would be costly.

Third, babies on a split-belt treadmill, where each foot gets its own belt. In two thousand five, researchers in Alberta supported seven- to twelve-month-old infants upright with their feet on the two belts. When one belt ran roughly seven to twenty-two times faster than the other, the fast leg could take extra steps while the slow leg stayed in stance. With the belts running in opposite directions, infants could step forward with one leg and backward with the other. Through all of it, the legs generally took turns swinging through the air. The authors suggest that each leg has its own pattern generator, and that the two interact so the legs take turns. Even before they can walk on their own, infants can make each leg follow a different stepping pattern while keeping the two legs coordinated.
